name: Lowry Theatre
description: Welcome aboard. You are joining us at Salford Quays, formerly known as the Manchester Docks. The building to the right is the Lowry Theatre and art gallery, opened in 2000 by Queen Elizabeth II.

name: Ontario Basin
description: The inner basin of Salford Quays. These docks once handled cotton, grain and timber from across the world; today they are the heart of the quayside watersports and waterside living.

name: Coronation Street & ITV
description: ITV and Coronation Street moved here in 2013. Coronation Street first aired on 9th December 1960 and holds the title of the world's longest-running TV soap.

name: Mode Wheel Locks
description: The last of five locks on the 35-mile journey from Eastham. Queen Victoria officially opened the Manchester Ship Canal here in 1894. Ships drop 18 metres to sea level.

name: Trafford Road Bridge
description: The swing bridge carrying Trafford Road over the Ship Canal. When large vessels passed, the roadway swung aside — a reminder that this was built as a working ship highway, not a pleasure lake.

name: Digital World Centre
description: One of the first office buildings of the new Salford Quays, completed in the late 1990s as the docks were remade into a media and business quarter.

name: Dock 10
description: Television studios on the water. The Dock 10 name comes from a 100-year-old plan to build a new dock here, abandoned with the First World War — revived as a studio complex a century later.

name: MediaCity / BBC
description: Home to the BBC, who relocated here in 2011. The studio complex is known as Dock 10 — from 100-year-old plans to build a new dock here, abandoned with the First World War.

name: Harbour City
description: Residential towers on the quayside, part of the 1980s–90s regeneration that turned working docks into a neighbourhood. The Metrolink stop of the same name sits a short walk inland.

name: Imperial Point
description: The glass office tower beside IWM North, a landmark on the Trafford Wharf skyline as the boat turns toward the museum and the stadium.

name: Imperial War Museum North
description: Designed by Daniel Libeskind in the deconstructivist style — imagined as three interlocking shards of a globe shattered by conflict. Opened July 2002.

name: Trafford Wharf
description: The stadium-end of the Ship Canal, beside IWM North. Matchday ferries arrive here — a short walk to Old Trafford.

name: Old Trafford Cricket Ground
description: Home of Lancashire County Cricket Club since 1864, and a Test match venue. The ground sits just inland of the canal, a neighbour to the football stadium.

name: Old Trafford
description: Home to Manchester United since 1910. Record attendance of 76,962 in 1939 for an FA Cup semi-final between Wolverhampton Wanderers and Grimsby Town.

name: Ordsall Chord
description: The curved railway viaduct opened in 2017, linking Piccadilly and Victoria stations. Network Rail's first new urban railway in Manchester for a century, spanning the Irwell.

name: Pomona Island
description: Once Pomona Docks, named for the Roman goddess of fruit trees. The island sat derelict for decades after the docks closed and is now being rebuilt as waterside homes.

name: Clippers Quay
description: A 1980s waterside housing development on the old docks — among the first residential schemes to colonise the Ship Canal after commercial shipping ended.

name: Soapworks
description: Once the Ivy Soap Works, established 1874. Acquired by Colgate-Palmolive in 1938. The preserved red brick chimney is a reminder of Salford's soap-making heritage.

name: Woden Street Footbridge
description: A pedestrian crossing over the Irwell between Ordsall and Old Trafford. From the water you can see how tightly the city presses against the old industrial river.

name: Regent Road
description: The dual carriageway bridging the water on the approach to the city. A working road over a working river — Manchester never quite hid its industry.

name: Ordsall Hall
description: A Tudor manor house a short walk from the water, home of the Radclyffe family for 300 years. One of Salford's oldest buildings, now a museum.

name: Hampson Street Wharf
description: Former timber and coal wharves on the Salford bank. The brick warehouses here were built to unload cargoes that had come up the Ship Canal from the Mersey.

name: Mark Addy Bridge
description: Named after local hero Mark Addy, who saved over 50 people from the polluted River Irwell in the 19th century. Also marks the boundary between the Ship Canal and the River Irwell.

name: Middlewood Locks
description: A new canalside neighbourhood on former railway land, where the River Irwell meets the city fringe. Apartments and public realm replacing the old goods yards.

name: Trinity Islands
description: One of Manchester's most recent residential developments, with towers rising up to 69 storeys. Part of the reason the city skyline is nicknamed MancHatten.

name: Deansgate Square
description: Four towers at the south end of Deansgate, including South Tower — among the tallest residential buildings in the UK. The skyline that earned Manchester the MancHatten nickname.

name: Beetham Tower
description: Completed in 2006, for a time the tallest building in the UK outside London. The Hilton occupies the lower floors; the distinctive cantilever is the hotel's sky bar.

name: Spinningfields
description: Manchester's business district on the site of former spinning mills. Civil Justice Centre's scooped facade is the landmark from the water.

name: Manchester Central
description: The former Central railway station, closed in 1969 and reborn as a conference hall. The great iron-and-glass roof is a Victorian train shed in a new life.

name: Great Northern Warehouse
description: A vast railway goods warehouse of 1898, built so trains could unload directly into the building. Now leisure and offices — the brick cliffs still read as industrial Manchester.

name: Science and Industry Museum
description: On the site of the world's first passenger railway station. The museum tells the story of Manchester as the original modern city — steam, cotton, computing.

name: Liverpool Road Station
description: Opened 1830 as the Manchester terminus of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway — the world's first inter-city passenger railway. The station buildings still stand.

name: Stephenson's Bridge
description: A Grade II listed stone bridge from 1830. Part of the world's first passenger railway line connecting Manchester to Liverpool, departing from nearby Liverpool Road Station.

name: Castlefield Viaducts
description: Layer upon layer of railway viaducts over the canal basin. Castlefield is where canal, rail and river meet — the junction that made Manchester.

name: Potato Wharf
description: Named for the cargo it handled. Barges unloaded potatoes and produce for the city markets here; the basin is now a quiet corner of Castlefield.

name: Hulme Lock
description: The junction with the Bridgewater Canal, Britain's first true industrial canal (1761). From here goods could move between the Ship Canal, the Irwell and the wider canal network.

name: Graffiti Palace
description: A stretch of riverside wall that has become an ever-changing canvas of street art. Artists from across Manchester come here to leave their mark — always evolving.

name: Knott Mill
description: An old mill district on the Medlock, just off the Irwell. Converted warehouses and a Metrolink stop — industry turned neighbourhood, a pattern you see all along this water.

name: Deansgate Locks
description: Bars and clubs under the railway arches beside the canal. After dark this is one of Manchester's best-known nightlife strips — by day, Victorian brick and iron.

name: Whitworth Street West
description: Warehouse canyon of the 19th-century cotton trade. The street runs parallel to the water; from the boat you see the backs of the mills that made Manchester's fortune.

name: Castlefield Basin
description: The historic canal basin where the Bridgewater Canal arrived in Manchester. Roman Mamucium stood on the sandstone bluff above — the city's name starts here.

name: Salford Quays return
description: The boat turns back toward the Quays. MediaCity, The Lowry and the footbridge come into view as the Ship Canal opens out again.

name: Quay West
description: A glass-fronted office block built in the early 1990s, once home to Peel Holdings who own the Manchester Ship Canal. Marks the end of your journey through Manchester's waterfront.
